subtopics.title: AC terms, instantaneous value, electrical degrees
subtopics.theory_md:
An alternating quantity reverses direction and varies in magnitude periodically: $v = V_m\sin\omega t$, with $\omega = 2\pi f$ rad/s and $T = 1/f$. **Cycle**: one complete set of values (360 electrical degrees). **Amplitude**: the peak $V_m$. **Instantaneous value**: $v$ at a given $t$ (put $\omega t$ in radians).

In a $P$-pole machine, $\theta_{elec} = \dfrac{P}{2}\,\theta_{mech}$ and $f = \dfrac{PN}{120}$ ($N$ in rpm).

To find the time to reach a value, solve $\sin\omega t = v/V_m$ and take the first angle.
subtopics.basics_md: A coil spinning in a magnetic field gives a voltage that rises, falls, reverses and repeats. One full turn of the coil in a two-pole field is one full cycle. Frequency is how many cycles per second; the period is the time for one.
key_points: Alternating quantity: changes magnitude and direction periodically; $\omega = 2\pi f$, $T = 1/f$
Cycle, amplitude (peak), time period, frequency defined with units
$\theta_{elec} = (P/2)\,\theta_{mech}$; a 4-pole machine gives 2 cycles per revolution
Instantaneous value: substitute $t$ with $\omega t$ in radians

subtopics.title: RMS and average value of a sine wave
subtopics.theory_md:
**RMS value**: the steady value that gives the same heating in a resistor, $V_{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac1T\int_0^T v^2\,dt}$. **Average value** $=\dfrac1T\int_0^T v\,dt$; for a symmetrical wave the full-cycle average is zero, so it is taken over a half cycle.

For $v = V_m\sin\omega t$:
- $V_{rms} = \dfrac{V_m}{\sqrt2} = 0.707V_m$ (use $\sin^2\theta = \tfrac{1-\cos2\theta}{2}$)
- $V_{av} = \dfrac{2V_m}{\pi} = 0.637V_m$ (half cycle)
- Form factor $= V_{rms}/V_{av} = 1.11$, peak factor $= V_m/V_{rms} = 1.414$.

These ratios hold only for a sine.
subtopics.basics_md: An AC and a DC supply can heat the same heater equally. The DC value that matches is the RMS value, which is why a "230 V" supply is 230 V RMS and its peak is higher, 325 V.
key_points: RMS = square root of the mean of the square (heating-effect definition)
Sine: $V_{rms} = V_m/\sqrt2$, $V_{av}$ (half cycle) $= 2V_m/\pi$
Form factor 1.11, peak factor 1.414 for a sine
Full-cycle average of a symmetrical wave is zero

questions.q: Derive the RMS value of $v = V_m\sin\omega t$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$V_{rms}^2 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}V_m^2\sin^2\theta\,d\theta = \dfrac{V_m^2}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\dfrac{1-\cos2\theta}{2}\,d\theta$

$= \dfrac{V_m^2}{4\pi}\left[\theta - \dfrac{\sin2\theta}{2}\right]_0^{2\pi} = \dfrac{V_m^2}{4\pi}(2\pi) = \dfrac{V_m^2}{2}$

$$V_{rms} = \dfrac{V_m}{\sqrt2} = 0.707\,V_m$$

$I_{rms} = \sqrt{I_0^2 + (I_m/\sqrt2)^2} = \sqrt{25 + 50} = 8.66$ A

Full-cycle average $= 5$ A (the sine part averages to zero).

The RMS values are not added directly: $5 + 7.07 = 12.07$ A is wrong.
points: $I_{rms}^2$ = sum of squares of the parts
Average over a full cycle $= 5$ A

subtopics.title: RMS and average of non-sinusoidal waves
subtopics.theory_md:
For any periodic wave, integrate over **one full period**, including the zero portions:

$V_{av} = \dfrac1T\int_0^T v\,dt$ (area under the curve $/\,T$), $V_{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac1T\int_0^T v^2\,dt}$.

Method: write $v$ for each segment (constant, straight line, or $V_m\sin\theta$), integrate $v$ and $v^2$ segment by segment, add, divide by $T$.

Standard results: half-wave rectified sine $V_{av} = V_m/\pi$, $V_{rms} = V_m/2$. Straight ramp from $a$ to $b$: mean $(a+b)/2$, mean square $(a^2+ab+b^2)/3$. Never use $V_m/\sqrt2$ here.
subtopics.basics_md: RMS means: square it, average it, root it. Average means: area under the curve divided by the period. A flat zero stretch still counts in the period, so it lowers both values.
key_points: Integrate over the full period, zero portions included
Segment by segment: integrate $v$ for the average, $v^2$ for the RMS
Half-wave rectified sine: $V_{av} = V_m/\pi$, $V_{rms} = V_m/2$
$V_m/\sqrt2$ and $2V_m/\pi$ apply to a sine only

questions.q: A half-wave rectified sine has a peak of 100 V. Find the average value, RMS value and form factor.
questions.model_answer_md:
Over the period $2\pi$ only $0$ to $\pi$ is non-zero.

$V_{av} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^\pi 100\sin\theta\,d\theta = \dfrac{100\times2}{2\pi} = 31.83$ V

$V_{rms}^2 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^\pi 100^2\sin^2\theta\,d\theta = \dfrac{10^4}{2\pi}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 2500$, so $V_{rms} = 50$ V

Form factor $= 50/31.83 = 1.57$.

questions.q: A periodic voltage of period 6 ms rises linearly from 0 to 12 V in 0 to 4 ms and is 0 V from 4 to 6 ms. Find its average and RMS values.
questions.model_answer_md:
For $0<t<4$ ms: $v = 3t$ (V, $t$ in ms). For $4<t<6$: $v = 0$.

$V_{av} = \dfrac16\int_0^4 3t\,dt = \dfrac16\left[1.5t^2\right]_0^4 = \dfrac{24}{6} = 4$ V

$V_{rms}^2 = \dfrac16\int_0^4 9t^2\,dt = \dfrac16\left[3t^3\right]_0^4 = \dfrac{192}{6} = 32$

$V_{rms} = \sqrt{32} = 5.66$ V
points: Divide by the full period 6 ms
Segment: ramp $v = -4 + 7t/T$ over one period, then a vertical drop
$V_m/\sqrt2$ must not be used for a non-sinusoid
Read the period (5 ms) and each segment: 2 V for 3 ms, 1 V for 1 ms, ramp 1 V to $-2$ V for 1 ms

subtopics.title: Phasors, phase difference, lead and lag
subtopics.theory_md:
A **phasor** is a line representing a sinusoid of fixed frequency: its length is the amplitude (or RMS value) and its angle from the reference is the phase, rotating anticlockwise at $\omega$.

$v = V_m\sin(\omega t + \phi)$: $\phi > 0$ means $v$ **leads** the reference, $\phi < 0$ means it **lags**. Phase difference is the angle between two waves of the **same frequency**; the time shift is $\Delta t = \phi/\omega$.

Convert cosine to sine first: $\cos x = \sin(x + 90^\circ)$. For a given instantaneous value at $t=0$, $\phi = \sin^{-1}(v_0/V_m)$.
subtopics.basics_md: Two runners on a circular track at the same speed keep a fixed gap between them. The gap is the phase difference. The runner ahead leads; the one behind lags. A phasor is just a snapshot of the runner's position.
key_points: Phasor: rotating line, length = amplitude or RMS, angle = phase, anticlockwise at $\omega$
Leading = ahead (anticlockwise); lagging = behind; same frequency only
$\Delta t = \phi/\omega$
Convert cos to sin before comparing phases

subtopics.title: R, L, C response and parallel RLC phasors
subtopics.theory_md:
With the reference taken as the common quantity:

- **R**: $v$ and $i$ in phase, $V = IR$.
- **L**: $i$ lags $v$ by $90^\circ$, $V = IX_L$, $X_L = \omega L$.
- **C**: $i$ leads $v$ by $90^\circ$, $V = IX_C$, $X_C = 1/\omega C$.

In a **series** circuit $I$ is the reference. In a **parallel** circuit $V$ is the reference: $I_R$ in phase, $I_L$ lags $90^\circ$, $I_C$ leads $90^\circ$, and
$$I = \sqrt{I_R^2 + (I_C - I_L)^2}.$$
$I_C > I_L$: circuit leads; $I_L > I_C$: lags.
subtopics.basics_md: An inductor resists a change of current, so its current is late. A capacitor must be charged by a current before its voltage can rise, so its current is early. A resistor has no delay.
key_points: R in phase; L current lags $90^\circ$; C current leads $90^\circ$
Series: $I$ is the reference; parallel: $V$ is the reference
Parallel: $I = \sqrt{I_R^2+(I_C-I_L)^2}$, $I_L$ and $I_C$ oppose
Shorted C or open R changes the branch currents as the phasor diagram shows

subtopics.title: Instantaneous and average power
subtopics.theory_md:
With $v = V_m\sin\omega t$ and $i = I_m\sin(\omega t - \phi)$:
$$p = vi = \tfrac{V_mI_m}{2}\left[\cos\phi - \cos(2\omega t - \phi)\right]$$
The second term has frequency $2f$ and averages to zero, so
$$P = \dfrac{V_mI_m}{2}\cos\phi = VI\cos\phi = I^2R\ \text{(W)}$$
with $V, I$ RMS and $\phi$ the angle **between** $v$ and $i$.

Pure R: $\phi = 0$, $P = VI$. Pure L or C: $\phi = 90^\circ$, $P = 0$ (energy is stored and returned each quarter cycle). Capacitive reactance falls as $f$ rises.
subtopics.basics_md: Power is voltage times current at each instant. In a resistor both are positive together, so power is always positive. In an inductor or capacitor, the power is positive for a quarter cycle (energy stored) and negative the next (energy returned), so the average is zero.
key_points: $p = vi$ has an average part $VI\cos\phi$ and a part at double frequency averaging zero
$P = VI\cos\phi = I^2R$ with RMS values; $\phi$ is the angle between $v$ and $i$
Pure L or C: average power zero (energy exchanged, not consumed)
With peak values $P = \frac{V_mI_m}{2}\cos\phi$

subtopics.title: Power triangle, power factor, complex power
subtopics.theory_md:
- **Active power** $P = VI\cos\phi = I^2R$ (W): useful, converted to heat or work.
- **Reactive power** $Q = VI\sin\phi = I^2X$ (VAR): exchanged with L and C fields, does no work.
- **Apparent power** $S = VI = I^2Z$ (VA).

**Power triangle**: $S^2 = P^2 + Q^2$, $\cos\phi = P/S = R/Z$ is the **power factor**, stated lagging (inductive) or leading (capacitive).

**Complex power** $\bar S = \bar V\bar I^* = P + jQ$. A low pf means more current for the same $P$: higher $I^2R$ loss, thicker cables, larger kVA ratings.

**Q factor of a coil**: $Q = \omega L/R$.
subtopics.basics_md: Beer analogy: the liquid is real power, the foam is reactive power, and the glass holds both, which is apparent power. You pay for the liquid but the glass (the cable and the transformer) must carry the foam too. Power factor is liquid divided by glass.
key_points: $P = VI\cos\phi$ (W), $Q = VI\sin\phi$ (VAR), $S = VI$ (VA); $S^2 = P^2+Q^2$
Power factor $= \cos\phi = P/S = R/Z$, with lagging or leading
Low pf: larger current, more copper loss, larger kVA, poor regulation
Complex power $\bar S = \bar V\bar I^* = P + jQ$

questions.model_answer_md:

subtopics.title: Power and power factor of parallel and mixed loads
subtopics.theory_md:
Active and reactive powers **add** arithmetically (they are conserved); apparent powers do not.
$$P_T = P_1 + P_2,\quad Q_T = Q_1 + Q_2\ (\text{lagging } +,\ \text{leading } -),\quad S_T = \sqrt{P_T^2 + Q_T^2},\quad \text{pf} = P_T/S_T.$$

**Parallel branches**: the voltage is common. Find $Z_{eq}$, then $V = I\,Z_{eq}$, branch currents $I_k = V/|Z_k|$, branch powers $P_k = I_k^2R_k$, branch pf $= R_k/|Z_k|$. For a load of $P$ at power factor $\cos\phi$: $Q = P\tan\phi$.
subtopics.basics_md: Each load pulls a useful current (real part) and a reactive current. Real parts simply add. Reactive parts of opposite kinds (inductive and capacitive) partly cancel, which is how a capacitor improves the pf.
key_points: $P_T = \sum P$, $Q_T = \sum Q$ with signs; $S_T = \sqrt{P_T^2+Q_T^2}$
Parallel: common $V$; $I_k = V/|Z_k|$, $P_k = I_k^2R_k$, pf$_k = R_k/|Z_k|$
Inductive branch lags, capacitive branch leads; state it

subtopics.title: Three-phase power and star-connected loads
subtopics.theory_md:
**Star**: $V_L = \sqrt3\,V_{ph}$, $I_L = I_{ph}$. **Delta**: $V_L = V_{ph}$, $I_L = \sqrt3\,I_{ph}$.

Power per phase $= V_{ph}I_{ph}\cos\phi$, with $\phi$ the angle between phase voltage and phase current. Total:
$$P = 3V_{ph}I_{ph}\cos\phi = \sqrt3\,V_LI_L\cos\phi,\qquad S = \sqrt3\,V_LI_L,\quad Q = \sqrt3\,V_LI_L\sin\phi.$$
Derivation in line values: star gives $V_{ph} = V_L/\sqrt3$, $I_{ph} = I_L$, so $3\cdot\dfrac{V_L}{\sqrt3}I_L\cos\phi = \sqrt3V_LI_L\cos\phi$.

$\cos\phi$ is **not** the angle between line voltage and line current.

subtopics.title: Series R, L, C: impedance, phase angle, power
subtopics.theory_md:
Take **current as the reference**. $V_R = IR$ (in phase), $V_L = IX_L$ (leads $I$ by $90^\circ$), $V_C = IX_C$ (lags $I$ by $90^\circ$), with $X_L = 2\pi fL$, $X_C = 1/2\pi fC$.

$V_L$ and $V_C$ oppose, so
$$V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2},\quad Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2},\quad \phi = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R}.$$
$I = V/Z$, $\cos\phi = R/Z$, $P = VI\cos\phi = I^2R$. $X_L > X_C$: current lags; $X_L < X_C$: leads; equal: in phase, pf = 1.

Instantaneous form: $v = V_m\sin\omega t$, $i = (V_m/Z)\sin(\omega t - \phi)$. Convert $\mu$F and mH to F and H.
subtopics.basics_md: Resistor voltage rides along with the current. Inductor voltage is ahead by a quarter turn and capacitor voltage is behind by a quarter turn, so the two fight each other. What is left of the fight, together with the resistor voltage, forms a right triangle.
key_points: Phasor diagram with $I$ horizontal; $V_R$ along it, $V_L$ up, $V_C$ down
$Z = \sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$, $\phi = \tan^{-1}[(X_L-X_C)/R]$, $\cos\phi = R/Z$
$X_L>X_C$ lagging, $X_L<X_C$ leading, equal gives resonance
$P = VI\cos\phi = I^2R$; only R consumes power
Voltages add as phasors; $V_L$ or $V_C$ can exceed $V$

questions.q: A series circuit of $R = 30\ \Omega$, $L = 0.2$ H and $C = 100\ \mu$F is connected to 200 V, 50 Hz. Find the current, phase angle, power factor and power.

questions.q: For a series R-L-C circuit state, with the phasor relation, how the current compares with the voltage when (i) $X_L>X_C$, (ii) $X_L<X_C$, (iii) $X_L=X_C$.
questions.model_answer_md:
(i) $X_L > X_C$: $V_L > V_C$, circuit inductive, current **lags** $V$ by $\phi = \tan^{-1}\frac{X_L-X_C}{R}$, pf lagging.

(ii) $X_L < X_C$: circuit capacitive, current **leads** $V$, pf leading.

(iii) $X_L = X_C$: $V_L = V_C$ cancel, $Z = R$, current in phase with $V$, pf unity, current maximum (series resonance).

points: Phasor diagram: $I$ reference; $V_R = IR$, $V_L = IX_L$ up, $V_C = IX_C$ down; $V = \sqrt{V_R^2+(V_L-V_C)^2}$
Series resonance: $X_L = X_C$, $Z = R$, current maximum, pf 1, $f_r = 1/2\pi\sqrt{LC}$
At series resonance $X_L = X_C$, so $\phi = \tan^{-1}0 = 0$ and $\cos\phi = R/Z = 1$: pf unity
$X_L = 300\times0.01 = 3\ \Omega$, so the net reactance must be capacitive: $X_C = 3+20 = 23\ \Omega$
$C = 1/(300\times23) = 144.9\ \mu$F (as printed; with $\omega = 3000$ rad/s the textbook value is $6.67\ \mu$F)
Zero phase difference needs net reactance zero: add a capacitor in series with $X_C = X_L = 1\ \Omega$

subtopics.title: Several impedances in series
subtopics.theory_md:
Impedances in series add as **complex numbers**: $\bar Z = \sum(R_k + jX_k)$, with $X_L$ positive and $X_C$ negative. So $R_T = \sum R$, $X_T = \sum X$, $Z = \sqrt{R_T^2 + X_T^2}$.

$I = V/Z$, the same in every part. The voltage across part $k$ is $V_k = I\,|Z_k|$, and it leads $I$ by $\tan^{-1}(X_k/R_k)$. The part voltages add as **phasors**, not arithmetically. Each part's pf is $R_k/|Z_k|$; the circuit pf is $R_T/Z$; $P = I^2R_T$.

Series-parallel reduction at $\omega$: $Z_L = j\omega L$, $Z_C = 1/(j\omega C)$.
subtopics.basics_md: A string of different resistors, coils and capacitors behaves like one single equivalent element. Add all the resistive parts together and all the reactive parts together, with coil reactance counted positive and capacitor reactance negative.
key_points: Add impedances as complex numbers: $R_T=\sum R$, $X_T=\sum X$
$X_L$ positive, $X_C$ negative; $Z=\sqrt{R_T^2+X_T^2}$
Same $I$ everywhere; $V_k = I|Z_k|$; voltages add as phasors
Pf of each part $R_k/|Z_k|$; circuit pf $R_T/Z$; $P=I^2R_T$

$Z = \dfrac{Z_LZ_C}{Z_L + Z_C} = \dfrac{(j25)(-j20)}{j5} = \dfrac{500}{j5} = -j100\ \Omega$ (capacitive)

(iii) pf $= 30/34.26 = 0.876$ leading; phasor diagram with $I$ horizontal, $V_1$ up at $57.5^\circ$, $V_2$ down at $58.2^\circ$
(iii) pf$_1 = 15/19.57 = 0.767$ lagging, pf$_2 = 0.999$ (leading, almost unity), total pf $= 25/27.8 = 0.899$ lagging
With c and d shorted: ($-j200$ in parallel with $j25$) $= j28.57$, in series with $-j100$ gives $-j71.43$
In parallel with the upper $j25$: $Z_{ab} = j38.46\ \Omega$

subtopics.title: Coil with resistance: voltage method
subtopics.theory_md:
A real coil (iron-cored choke) has resistance $r$ as well as reactance. If measured voltages do not add for ideal elements, split the coil voltage into $V_r = Ir$ (in phase with $I$) and $V_X = IX_L$ (leads $I$ by $90^\circ$).

With $I$ as reference and a voltmeter reading across R, the coil and C:
1. $V_r^2 + V_X^2 = V_{coil}^2$
2. $(V_R + V_r)^2 + (V_X - V_C)^2 = V^2$ (or, for R and coil only, $(V_R+V_r)^2 + V_X^2 = V_{R+coil}^2$)

Solve for $V_r$, $V_X$. Then coil pf $= V_r/V_{coil}$, circuit pf $= (V_R+V_r)/V$, coil loss $= V_rI$, $f = 1/(2\pi CX_C)$ with $X_C = V_C/I$.
subtopics.basics_md: If readings of a resistor, a coil and a capacitor in series add up in a way that breaks the rules, the coil is hiding a resistance. Treat the coil as a small resistor in series with a pure inductor, and let the phasor triangle find the hidden part.
key_points: Coil voltage splits into $V_r$ (with $I$) and $V_X$ (ahead by $90^\circ$)
Two equations from the voltage triangle give $V_r$ and $V_X$
Coil pf $=V_r/V_{coil}$; circuit pf $=(V_R+V_r)/V$; coil loss $V_rI$
$X_C = V_C/I$ gives frequency or $C$

questions.q: The loss in an iron-cored choke carrying current $I$ is given by
questions.why: Only the component in phase with $I$ does work.

questions.q: A resistor, coil and capacitor in series read 82 V, 50 V and 20 V across a 100 V supply. Why do the readings not simply add?
options: they are phasors, and the coil also has resistance
questions.why: Voltages are $90^\circ$ or $180^\circ$ apart and the coil voltage has an in-phase part.

questions.q: A resistor, a coil and a capacitor in series carry 2 A across a 100 V supply. The voltages are 82 V across the resistor, 50 V across the coil and 20 V across the capacitor. Find the power factor of the coil and of the circuit, the coil resistance and the power taken.
questions.model_answer_md:
Coil: $V_r^2 + V_X^2 = 50^2$ (1)

Circuit: $(82 + V_r)^2 + (V_X - 20)^2 = 100^2$ (2)

Expand (2) and use (1): $164V_r - 40V_X = 376$, so $V_X = 4.1V_r - 9.4$. Put in (1):
$V_r = 14$ V, $V_X = 48$ V.

Coil pf $= 14/50 = 0.28$ lagging. Circuit pf $= (82+14)/100 = 0.96$ lagging ($V_X > V_C$).

Coil resistance $r = 14/2 = 7\ \Omega$. Power $P = VI\cos\phi = 100\times2\times0.96 = 192$ W (check: $I^2(R+r) = 4\times(41+7) = 192$ W).
points: Two equations from the voltage triangle
Coil pf $0.28$ lagging, circuit pf $0.96$ lagging
(ii) Loss in the inductor $= V_rI = 5.5\times0.345 = 1.90$ W

subtopics.title: Series resonance: condition and features
subtopics.theory_md:
A series R-L-C circuit is in **resonance** when the current is in phase with the supply voltage, i.e. $X_L = X_C$:
$$\omega_rL = \frac{1}{\omega_rC}\ \Rightarrow\ f_r = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$$
At resonance: $Z = R$ (minimum), $I = V/R$ (maximum), pf = 1, and $V_L = V_C = I X_L$, equal and opposite, often much **larger than the supply voltage**. Below $f_r$ the circuit is capacitive, above it is inductive. A coil with resistance has $V_{coil} = I\sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}$. Resonance is reached by varying $f$, $L$ or $C$.
subtopics.basics_md: A child on a swing goes highest when you push at the swing's own rhythm. In the circuit, the energy sloshes between the inductor and the capacitor at one natural frequency. When the supply matches it, only the resistor limits the current.
key_points: Condition $X_L = X_C$, $f_r = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$
At resonance $Z = R$ minimum, $I$ maximum, pf 1, $\phi = 0$
$V_L = V_C$, equal and opposite, can exceed the supply voltage
Below $f_r$ capacitive, above $f_r$ inductive

questions.q: At series resonance the impedance of the circuit is
questions.why: $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + 0} = R$; parallel resonance is the one with maximum impedance.

questions.q: The resonant frequency of a series circuit with $L = 1$ mH and $C = 1\ \mu$F is nearest to
questions.why: $f_r = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{10^{-9}}) = 5.03$ kHz; 31.6 krad/s is $\omega_r$, not $f_r$.

questions.q: State the condition of series resonance in an R-L-C circuit, derive the resonant frequency and list the features at resonance.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Condition**: current in phase with voltage, i.e. $X_L = X_C$.

**Derivation**: $\omega_rL = \dfrac{1}{\omega_rC}$, so $\omega_r = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$ and $f_r = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$.

**At resonance**
- $Z = R$, minimum; $I = V/R$, maximum
- pf = 1, $\phi = 0$
- $V_L = V_C = IX_L$, equal and opposite, may exceed $V$
- Below $f_r$ the circuit is capacitive, above it inductive.

questions.q: A series circuit has $R = 20\ \Omega$, $L = 50$ mH, $C = 20\ \mu$F and a 100 V variable-frequency supply. Find the resonant frequency, current and the voltage across L and C at resonance.
questions.model_answer_md:
$f_r = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{50\times10^{-3}\times20\times10^{-6}}} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\times10^{-3}} = 159.2$ Hz

$\omega_r = 1000$ rad/s, $X_L = X_C = 1000\times0.05 = 50\ \Omega$

$I = V/R = 100/20 = 5$ A

$V_L = V_C = 5\times50 = 250$ V (2.5 times the supply voltage, $Q = 2.5$).

points: Current maximum on varying L means resonance: $Z = R$

subtopics.title: Detuned circuits and tuning to a station
subtopics.theory_md:
For a fixed $R$, the resonance condition ties $f$, $L$ and $C$ together: $LC = 1/\omega_r^2$.

- **Tuning**: for a given $L$, $C = \dfrac{1}{\omega_r^2L}$. A different $f_r$ needs a different $C$; doubling $L$ at the same $f_r$ needs half the $C$.
- **Detuned** ($f \ne f_r$ or $L$, $C$ changed): $X = X_L - X_C \ne 0$, $Z = \sqrt{R^2+X^2}$, $\phi = \tan^{-1}(X/R)$; $X>0$ lagging, $X<0$ leading.
- **R shorted at resonance**: $Z \to 0$, the current is limited only by the source and winding resistance, and $V_L=V_C$ become dangerously large.
- Resonance can occur at another frequency $f_r$ even if the supply is 50 Hz: it needs $f=f_r$.
subtopics.basics_md: A radio dial changes C to move f_r to the station you want. If L is changed instead, C must change in the opposite proportion to keep the same f_r. Away from f_r the circuit leans inductive or capacitive and the current falls.
key_points: Tuning: $C = 1/(\omega_r^2L)$; $LC$ fixed for a given $f_r$
Away from resonance $Z=\sqrt{R^2+X^2}$, $\phi = \tan^{-1}(X/R)$
Doubling $L$ at the same $f_r$ means halving $C$
R shorted at resonance: very large current and voltages across L and C

questions.q: The resonant frequency of a series R-L-C circuit does not depend on
questions.why: $f_r = 1/2\pi\sqrt{LC}$ has no $R$; $R$ only sets the peak current and $Q$.

questions.q: A series circuit is tuned to resonance. If $L$ is now doubled at the same frequency, the circuit becomes
questions.why: $X_L$ doubles while $X_C$ is unchanged, so $X_L > X_C$.

questions.q: A tuning coil of 200 $\mu$H is to tune a receiver from 1 MHz to 1.5 MHz. Find the range of capacitance needed.
questions.model_answer_md:
$C = \dfrac{1}{(2\pi f)^2L}$

At 1 MHz: $C = \dfrac{1}{(2\pi\times10^6)^2\times200\times10^{-6}} = 126.7$ pF

At 1.5 MHz: $C = \dfrac{1}{(2\pi\times1.5\times10^6)^2\times200\times10^{-6}} = 56.3$ pF

So $C$ varies from 56.3 pF to 126.7 pF (higher frequency needs smaller $C$).

questions.q: A series circuit with $R = 25\ \Omega$, $L = 0.2$ H and $C = 20\ \mu$F is connected to 240 V, 50 Hz. Find the resonant frequency, the current and phase angle at 50 Hz, and the current at resonance.
questions.model_answer_md:
$f_r = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{0.2\times20\times10^{-6}}} = 79.6$ Hz

At 50 Hz: $X_L = 62.83\ \Omega$, $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\times50\times20\times10^{-6}} = 159.15\ \Omega$

$X = -96.3\ \Omega$ (capacitive), $Z = \sqrt{25^2 + 96.3^2} = 99.5\ \Omega$

$I = 240/99.5 = 2.41$ A leading, $\phi = \tan^{-1}(96.3/25) = 75.5^\circ$ (the circuit is below $f_r$).

At resonance $I = 240/25 = 9.6$ A in phase.

points: Comment: nearly purely inductive, current falls from 10 A to 0.38 A, pf $0.038$, resonance lost
Doubling L means halving C; current returns to 10 A at unity pf
$R = 240/10 = 24\ \Omega$; with R shorted, $Z = |X_L - X_C| = 0$ at resonance
Current $\to\infty$ (limited only by source and winding resistance); $V_L = V_C$ become very large, the fuse or breaker trips
At 50 Hz, $X_L \ne X_C$ for the C found (4.77 or 1.29 $\mu$F), so the circuit is not in resonance at 50 Hz
Resonance occurs at $f_r = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$: $32.6$ Hz for 4.77 $\mu$F, $62.7$ Hz for 1.29 $\mu$F
At 96 kHz: $C = 1/(\omega_r^2L) = 68.7$ pF (smaller than for 91 kHz)

subtopics.title: Q factor, bandwidth and half-power points
subtopics.theory_md:
**Q factor** (series): $Q = \dfrac{\omega_rL}{R} = \dfrac{1}{\omega_rCR} = \dfrac1R\sqrt{\dfrac LC}$ = voltage magnification: $V_L = V_C = QV$.

**Half-power points** $f_1, f_2$: where $I = I_0/\sqrt2$ (the **-3 dB** line), i.e. $P = P_{max}/2$ and $|X_L - X_C| = R$.

**Bandwidth** $BW = f_2 - f_1 = \dfrac{R}{2\pi L} = \dfrac{f_r}{Q}$ (Hz), and $f_r = \sqrt{f_1f_2}$.

Higher $R$: lower $Q$, wider bandwidth, flatter curve. Higher $Q$: sharper tuning and better selectivity.
subtopics.basics_md: Picture the current-versus-frequency curve as a hill. A tall narrow hill (high Q) picks out one station only. A low wide hill (low Q) lets several stations through. Bandwidth is the width of the hill at 70.7 percent of its height.
key_points: $Q = \omega_rL/R = (1/R)\sqrt{L/C}$, voltage magnification
Half-power points at $I_0/\sqrt2$, the $-3$ dB line, where $|X|=R$
$BW = f_2-f_1 = R/2\pi L = f_r/Q$
Larger $R$ lowers $Q$ and widens the band

questions.q: The bandwidth of a series resonant circuit is
questions.why: $BW = f_r/Q = R/2\pi L$.

questions.q: If the resistance of a series resonant circuit is increased, then
questions.why: $Q = \omega_rL/R$ falls and $BW = R/2\pi L$ rises.

questions.q: Define the Q factor of a series resonant circuit, its bandwidth and the -3 dB line. How are they related?
questions.model_answer_md:
**Q factor**: $Q = \omega_rL/R = \frac1R\sqrt{L/C}$; the voltage magnification, $V_L = V_C = QV$.

**-3 dB line**: drawn at $I = I_0/\sqrt2 = 0.707I_0$ on the resonance curve; there the power is half of the maximum. It cuts the curve at the half-power frequencies $f_1$ and $f_2$.

**Bandwidth**: $BW = f_2 - f_1 = R/2\pi L = f_r/Q$.

A high $Q$ gives a narrow band and a sharp (selective) response.

questions.q: A series circuit has $R = 20\ \Omega$, $L = 50$ mH and $C = 20\ \mu$F. Find $f_r$, $Q$, bandwidth and the half-power frequencies.
questions.model_answer_md:
$f_r = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} = 159.15$ Hz, $\omega_r = 1000$ rad/s

$Q = \dfrac{\omega_rL}{R} = \dfrac{1000\times0.05}{20} = 2.5$

$BW = \dfrac{f_r}{Q} = 63.66$ Hz (check: $R/2\pi L = 20/0.314 = 63.66$ Hz)

$f_{1,2} = \mp\dfrac{R}{4\pi L} + \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{R}{4\pi L}\right)^2 + f_r^2}$ with $R/4\pi L = 31.83$ Hz:

$f_1 = 130.5$ Hz, $f_2 = 194.1$ Hz (check $\sqrt{f_1f_2} = 159.15$ Hz).

points: -3 dB line at $I = I_0/\sqrt2 = 0.707I_0$, power half of the maximum; it cuts the curve at the half-power frequencies $f_1$, $f_2$
Bandwidth $= f_2 - f_1 = R/2\pi L = f_r/Q$
-3 dB line at $0.707I_0$ marks the half-power points $f_1$ and $f_2$ ($|X_L-X_C| = R$)
Bandwidth: the band of frequencies between them, $f_2-f_1 = f_r/Q$
Comment: $V_L = V_C = 10\times$ supply voltage (magnification), current maximum, pf 1

subtopics.title: Parallel resonance and the rejector circuit
subtopics.theory_md:
A coil ($R$, $L$) in parallel with $C$ is in resonance when the supply current is in phase with $V$: the coil's quadrature current equals $I_C$.
$$f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{1}{LC} - \frac{R^2}{L^2}} \approx \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}\ (\text{small } R).$$
At resonance the **dynamic impedance** $Z_D = \dfrac{L}{CR}$ is **maximum**, the line current is **minimum**, pf = 1.

**Q factor** $= \dfrac{\omega_0L}{R}$ = current magnification: circulating current $= Q\times$ line current.

It is a **rejector circuit**: its impedance is highest at $f_0$, so that frequency is blocked and others pass. Series resonance is the acceptor circuit.
subtopics.basics_md: A swing pushed by a tiny nudge each time keeps swinging with a big motion. In the parallel circuit a large current circulates between coil and capacitor while the supply only tops up the losses, so the line current is tiny at resonance.
key_points: Condition: supply current in phase with $V$; $f_0\approx1/2\pi\sqrt{LC}$
Dynamic impedance $L/CR$ maximum, line current minimum
Q = current magnification $\omega_0L/R$
Rejector because it opposes (rejects) the resonant frequency

questions.q: At parallel resonance the line current is
questions.why: Impedance is maximum, so the line current is minimum.

questions.q: A parallel resonant circuit is called a rejector circuit because at resonance it
options: offers maximum impedance to that frequency
questions.why: A very high $Z_D = L/CR$ stops that frequency from passing along the line.

questions.q: A coil of $R = 10\ \Omega$ and $L = 100\ \mu$H is in parallel with a 100 pF capacitor. Find the resonant frequency, the dynamic impedance and the Q factor.
questions.model_answer_md:
$f_0 \approx \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{10^{-4}\times10^{-10}}} = 1.59$ MHz (the $R^2/L^2 = 10^{10}$ term is negligible against $1/LC = 10^{14}$).

$Z_D = \dfrac{L}{CR} = \dfrac{10^{-4}}{10^{-10}\times10} = 10^5\ \Omega = 100\ \text{k}\Omega$

$Q = \dfrac{\omega_0L}{R} = \dfrac{10^7\times10^{-4}}{10} = 100$

points: Parallel resonance: coil ($R$, $L$) in parallel with $C$; condition: supply current in phase with $V$, $f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{1}{LC}-\frac{R^2}{L^2}}$
At resonance $Z_D = L/CR$ is maximum, line current minimum, pf unity
Q factor $=\omega_0L/R$: current magnification, circulating current $= Q\times$ line current; higher Q gives narrower bandwidth
Rejector circuit: maximum impedance at $f_0$ means the resonant frequency is rejected (blocked) from the line
